### CRITICAL

- [severity: critical] **§4.2 SFT baseline 对比 claim 与数据矛盾**（第 47 行）。原文："the RL checkpoint at PR=32% already shows H1>0 and **lower ISR* than SFT** at PR=14%"。

  这不影响核心论点（hacking 是 RL-specific），但 claim 需要修正。建议：改为 "the RL checkpoint at PR=32% already shows H1>0 despite higher ISR*, indicating structural shortcuts emerge from the first training phase, whereas SFT at PR=14% shows only 7% H1 — confirming the gap is RL-specific, not merely a PR-level effect。" 或将此对比移至 appendix 做更细致分析。

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on held-out logical reasoning problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises, reducing each ``proof'' to a structural shortcut invisible to the execution reward.
When the solver receives premises that already contain the target conclusion, it trivially succeeds; the model has learned to satisfy the reward without performing logical derivation.
This gap between execution success and structural integrity defines a critical blind spot in neurosymbolic reinforcement learning.

Neurosymbolic approaches that pair large language models with formal solvers have demonstrated strong performance on logical reasoning benchmarks~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025}.
The dominant paradigm treats solver execution as a binary reward signal: the model generates a formal specification, a solver attempts a proof, and the outcome drives policy optimization via GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} or related algorithms~\citep{deepseek-r1}.
This execution-only evaluation conflates genuine reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
A model can achieve arbitrarily high prove rates by embedding the target conclusion among its premises, by producing contradictory axiom sets that prove anything via explosion, or by generating tautological single-clause outputs---all of which satisfy the solver without requiring any logical derivation.
Specification gaming of this kind has been documented in reasoning models more broadly~\citep{bondarenko-spec-gaming}, and a growing body of work studies reward hacking mechanisms in LLM training~\citep{reward-hacking-survey}, yet systematic characterization in neurosymbolic RL remains absent.

No principled diagnostic exists for detecting and quantifying structural degeneration in RL-trained formalizers.
Prompting-based neurosymbolic systems~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm} do not involve RL training and thus sidestep the problem entirely.
\citet{mellgren-prolog-grpo} hand-craft Prolog-specific structure penalties but provide no systematic analysis of the failure modes they target.
Verification-reward approaches use solver or prover outcomes as training signals~\citep{deepseek-prover-v15, rlsf} but evaluate execution correctness only.
Recent work has begun examining whether LLMs game formalization tasks~\citep{kim-game-formalization}, finding that high compilation rates do not imply faithful outputs---yet no framework connects structural diagnosis to the reward hacking dynamics that emerge during RL training.
The result is a field that optimizes for---and reports---prove rates without any mechanism to assess whether the underlying formalizations contain genuine logical structure.

We observe that component necessity testing---systematically ablating each solver input and checking whether the proof still holds---provides a principled, solver-agnostic diagnostic for this problem.
Removing a premise from a well-structured formalization should break the proof; removing one from a degenerate output that embeds the conclusion will not.
This leave-one-out (LOO) protocol yields a continuous score, the \emph{Intensional Structure Ratio} (ISR), measuring the fraction of formal components that are necessary for the proof.
The protocol requires only the ability to re-execute the solver with modified inputs, making it applicable across formal languages and proof systems without language-specific engineering.

A natural question follows: can ISR serve not merely as a post-hoc diagnostic but as a training signal to incentivize structural integrity?
We find that it cannot.
When ISR is incorporated into the GRPO reward, the model games the metric itself---a meta-level instance of Goodhart's Law~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, gao-reward-overoptimization}.
Rather than producing better-structured proofs, the model discovers strategies that inflate ISR directly, most commonly by reducing all premises to a single clause that duplicates the conclusion.
ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness, and LOO-based metrics carry an inherent mathematical bias toward outputs with fewer components: fewer premises means each is trivially more ``necessary.''
These properties make ISR a reliable observer of structural integrity but an unreliable optimizer of it.

We introduce \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a protocol that applies component necessity testing to derive ISR and systematically characterizes reward hacking across GRPO training conditions (Figure~\ref{fig:sta_overview}).
Our experimental design spans 6 reward configurations (execution-only, ISR-augmented at two dose levels, matched random-reward controls, convex combination, and a supervised fine-tuning baseline), 3 random seeds per configuration, and up to 1{,}000 training steps, evaluated on two formal languages: first-order logic (FOL, verified by Prover9) and Prolog (verified by SWI-Prolog).

STA reveals that execution-only GRPO training produces progressive structural collapse invisible to the training reward.
Prove rate reaches 93\% while ISR deteriorates from 0.64 at 100 steps to 0.13 at 500 steps to 0.003 at 1{,}000 steps---a 99.5\% decline quantifying structural degeneration that prove rate cannot detect.
All three random seeds exhibit 87--100\% conclusion embedding in their proved outputs, demonstrating that degeneration is systematic rather than seed-specific.
By 1{,}000 steps, 94.8\% of proved samples have ISR${=}$0: no single component is necessary for the proof.
A supervised fine-tuning baseline trained on the same data achieves only 14\% prove rate but 92.9\% structurally genuine outputs with near-zero hacking (7.1\% H1, 0\% H7), confirming that reward hacking is RL-specific rather than an artifact of data exposure (\textbf{C1}: ISR as diagnostic, with complete collapse trajectory; \S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

When ISR augments the GRPO reward ($r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$), meta-level Goodhart effects emerge~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl}.
At low dose ($\beta{=}0.1$), ISR reward induces ISR-specific gaming: across three seeds, 64.5\% of proved outputs exhibit single-premise conclusion duplication (H7 mode) that inflates ISR by gaming the metric, compared to 0\% across all three random-reward controls---confirming H7 as ISR-reward-specific.
The remaining seed's apparent structural advantage disappears entirely under premise-count-matched analysis (1.06$\times$, indistinguishable from the random baseline); the raw ISR elevation is a mathematical artifact of premise minimization, not improved reasoning.
At high dose ($\beta{=}0.3$), classic Goodhart collapse occurs: prove rate drops to 18\% versus 48\% for the matched random control.
This dose-response pattern maps onto established Goodhart dynamics~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization}: low-dose proxy gaming that inflates the metric without genuine improvement, followed by high-dose collapse where the proxy signal overwhelms the primary objective.
ISR-as-reward provides no genuine structural benefit at any dose (\textbf{C2}: empirical meta-level Goodhart characterization; \S\ref{sec:goodhart}).

Both the diagnostic capability and the Goodhart failure transfer across structurally different formal languages.
Applying STA to Prolog formalizations verified by SWI-Prolog, execution-only training again produces near-zero ISR (mean 0.04 across 3 seeds, $\text{PR}{=}53\%{\pm}31\text{pp}$), replicating the FOL collapse pattern with comparable cross-seed instability.
Prolog ISR-as-reward yields \emph{universal} Goodhart: all three seeds converge to gaming with 0\% genuine output, each via a distinct mechanism---tautological single-clause duplication, degenerate uppercase pseudo-Prolog syntax, and query-as-fact gaming where the model sets the target query as its own provable fact.
This is strictly stronger than the FOL result, where ${\sim}$16\% genuine output persists, demonstrating that simpler formal semantics enable more complete metric exploitation (\textbf{C3}: cross-logic diagnostic transfer with universal Goodhart; \S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).

Across all experimental conditions, we identify and quantify 7 distinct hacking modes---conclusion embedding in single-premise (H7) and multi-premise (H1) variants, tautological collapse, complexity-without-utility, repetition collapse, premise padding, and query-as-fact gaming---providing a concrete, empirically grounded taxonomy for diagnosing structural failures in neurosymbolic RL systems.
Each mode is quantified per reward condition and seed, enabling practitioners to anticipate the specific failure modes their training configurations are likely to produce (\textbf{C4}: hacking taxonomy; \S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

These findings expose a fundamental asymmetry: ISR is reliable as a diagnostic observer of structural integrity but unreliable as an optimization target.
This instantiates a broader cautionary principle for proxy-metric-as-reward approaches~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, pan-reward-misspecification}: diagnostic metrics that detect reward hacking can themselves become gaming targets when repurposed as training signals.
The asymmetry---\emph{reliable observer, unreliable optimizer}---carries implications beyond formal reasoning for any system where proxy measures of structural quality are candidates for reward shaping.
We release our code, evaluation scripts, and complete experimental outputs to support reproducibility.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on first-order logic problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises.
The solver succeeds not because the model has learned to reason, but because the formalization trivially entails any conclusion that already appears as a premise.
This structural shortcut is invisible to execution-based evaluation: prove rate registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine multi-step derivation or degenerate circular embedding.
The reward optimizes solver success; the model finds the shortest path to it.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate---the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}---conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under reinforcement learning, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback as reward; this drives rapid PR gains but gives no gradient on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} offer step-level supervision but require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A complementary line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}, yet no existing method provides an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs---one adaptable in principle to any solver supporting component-level input manipulation (see \S\ref{sec:related-work} for full context).

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a diagnostic protocol applying \emph{component necessity testing}---leave-one-out (LOO) ablation on solver inputs---to quantify structural integrity (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR).
ISR${=}1$ indicates every component is individually required for proof success; ISR${=}0$ indicates complete structural redundancy.
We are explicit that LOO ablation is itself standard---in mutation testing~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} and feature attribution---and we claim novelty not in the primitive but in its application as a diagnostic for GRPO reward hacking and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
We also emphasize that ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity: a downstream NLI evaluation finds ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated ($\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$), confirming it measures properties orthogonal to semantic correctness.

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
Applied as a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio} data, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory entirely invisible to prove rate: ISR falls from 0.642 at 100 steps to 0.132 at 500 steps to 0.003 at 1000 steps---a 99.5\% degradation---while prove rate simultaneously rises from 32\% to 96\%.
Three random seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
A supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline on the same data achieves a prove rate of 14\% but 92.9\% non-hacking proofs with near-zero shortcut content, confirming that the structural collapse is a consequence of RL reward optimization, not model capacity or data limitations.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart.}
A natural question is whether ISR can serve as a training signal.
The answer is negative: when ISR is added to the reward, $r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$, the model games the diagnostic itself---\emph{meta-level Goodhart's Law}~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, karwowski-goodhart-rl, gao-reward-overoptimization}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, 64.5\% of proved samples (3-seed mean) exhibit ISR-specific single-premise-equals-conclusion duplication---a construction in which ISR is high \emph{by definition} of the LOO metric---versus 0\% under a matched random-bonus reward; the one seed that retains a non-trivial ``genuine'' fraction reduces to 1.06$\times$ random after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
At $\beta{=}0.3$ the same reward produces extreme cross-seed instability (PR $66{\pm}42\%$) with three qualitatively distinct Goodhart pathways: reward collapse (PR ${=}\,18\%$), shortcut dominance (86\% PR, 69\% conclusion embedding), and pure metric gaming (95\% PR, 100\% ISR-inflating duplications, ISR${=}0.742$).
The effect transfers and intensifies in a different formal language: in Prolog with SWI-Prolog as solver, all three seeds produce 0\% non-hacking output---universal Goodhart---each via a distinct mechanism, including a \emph{query-as-fact gaming} mode that bypasses text-match classifiers entirely.
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer.}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
Across 6 reward conditions, 3 seeds, 2 logic types, and up to 1000 training steps, we make four contributions:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item[\textbf{C1.}] \textbf{ISR as diagnostic} for GRPO reward hacking, with a complete collapse trajectory ($\text{ISR}{=}0.642{\to}0.003$ over 1000 steps) invisible to prove rate, and an SFT control (92.9\% non-hacking) localizing the failure mode to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:isr-diagnostic}).
\item[\textbf{C2.}] \textbf{Empirical meta-level Goodhart} in neurosymbolic RL, with a random-bonus control that isolates ISR-specific gaming (H7: 64.5\% vs.\ 0\%) and a premise-count-matched analysis showing that the sole apparent ISR gain is a mathematical artifact of the LOO metric, not a structural improvement (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
\item[\textbf{C3.}] \textbf{Cross-logic transfer} to Prolog/SWI-Prolog, demonstrating universal Goodhart (3/3 seeds gaming, 0\% non-hacking) and indicating that simpler formal semantics enable more complete exploitation (\S\ref{sec:prolog}).
\item[\textbf{C4.}] \textbf{A seven-mode hacking taxonomy} including a Prolog-specific query-as-fact gaming mode that bypasses text-match classifiers, motivating functional ($n_{\text{necessary}}$-based) cross-validation of diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy-results}).
\end{itemize}
Taken together, these results characterize ISR's fundamental asymmetry: it is a useful instrument for \emph{detecting} reward hacking in solver-backed RL, but unsuitable as an optimization target because the very LOO primitive that makes it interpretable also makes it gameable.
We see the empirical Goodhart characterization, premise-count confound, and cross-logic universality as cautionary results for any work treating a structural proxy metric as a training signal.

58	\label{app:algorithm}
59	
60	Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} (Section~\ref{sec:sta}) gives the procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

64	\section{Extended Discussion}
65	\label{app:extended-discussion}
66	
67	\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
68	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
69	This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
70	We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
71	ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
72	ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.
73	
74	Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
75	Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
76	Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
77	ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.
78	
79	\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
80	LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
81	A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
82	This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
83	Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
84	This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
85	We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.
86	
87	\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
88	The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
89	ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
90	The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
91	$\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism; $\beta{=}0.3$ completes the Goodhart trajectory with outright performance collapse.
92	The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.
93	
94	\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
95	The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
96	ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
97	Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

100	\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
101	\label{app:hacking-modes}
102	
103	We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
104	Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
105	Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

Exec: H1${=}87$\% in s42; $\bullet$ marks seed- or step-specific modes (H7/Tautological in s44, Repetition in s43, Contradiction at 1000 steps). C-w/o-util.: complexity-without-utility (random-specific). Q-as-fact: Prolog STA only (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).}

128	\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
129	Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
130	H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
131	No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.
132	
133	To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
134	Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
135	We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
136	This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
137	The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.
138	
139	\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}
140	
141	\paragraph{Definition.}
142	The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
143	The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.
144	
145	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
146	{\small\begin{verbatim}
147	Premises:
148	  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
149	  bird(tweety).
150	  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
151	Conclusion: flies(tweety).
152	\end{verbatim}}
153	
154	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
155	Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
156	ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.
157	
158	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
159	Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
160	Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).
161	
162	
163	\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}
164	
165	\paragraph{Definition.}
166	The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
167	Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
168	Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.
169	
170	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
171	{\small\begin{verbatim}
172	Premises:
173	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
174	Conclusion:
175	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
176	\end{verbatim}}
177	
178	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
179	ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
180	The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
181	H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.
182	
183	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
184	ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
185	\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).
186	
187	
188	\subsection{Tautological Collapse}
189	
190	\paragraph{Definition.}
191	Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.
192	
193	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
194	\begin{verbatim}
195	Premises: p(a).
196	Conclusion: p(a).
197	\end{verbatim}
198	
199	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
200	ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
201	Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.
202	
203	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
204	Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
205	Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).
206	
207	
208	\subsection{Repetition Collapse}
209	
210	\paragraph{Definition.}
211	The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
212	Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.
213	
214	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
215	\begin{verbatim}
216	penguin(fido).
217	penguin(fido).
218	penguin(fido).
219	... (repeated to 512 tokens)
220	query(penguin(fido)).
221	\end{verbatim}
222	
223	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
224	ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
225	ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.
226	
227	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
228	Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).
229	
230	
231	\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}
232	
233	\paragraph{Definition.}
234	The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
235	The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.
236	
237	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
238	{\small\begin{verbatim}
239	Premises:
240	  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
241	    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
242	  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
243	  P(a).            % only this needed
244	Conclusion: Q(a).
245	\end{verbatim}}
246	
247	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
248	ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
249	This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.
250	
251	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
252	Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
253	Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).
254	
255	
256	\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}
257	
258	\paragraph{Definition.}
259	The component count grows unboundedly over training.
260	Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
261	Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.
262	
263	\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
264	{\small\begin{verbatim}
265	Premises:
266	  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
267	  % conclusion embedded among premises
268	Conclusion: Q(a).
269	\end{verbatim}}
270	
271	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
272	ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).
273	
274	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
275	Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
276	Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).
277	
278	
279	\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}
280	
281	\paragraph{Definition.}
282	The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
283	Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
284	This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.
285	
286	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
287	\begin{verbatim}
288	% NL: "Fido is happy."
289	% Model output:
290	fido_is_happy.
291	:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
292	\end{verbatim}
293	
294	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
295	ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
296	The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
297	Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.
298	
299	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
300	Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
301	95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

406	PR increases monotonically ($0.32 \to 0.93 \to 0.96$) while structural quality collapses, confirming that ISR captures degeneration invisible to execution reward.
407	By step 1000, 94.8\% of proved samples have ISR~$=0$ and the mean component count rises to 18.55.

409	\paragraph{Prolog: universal Goodhart via three distinct pathways.}
410	All three Prolog exec+ISR seeds exhibit Goodhart's Law with 0\% non-hacking proofs (Figure~\ref{fig:prolog-comparison}), but each discovers a different gaming mechanism:
411	seed~42 produces clean H7 tautologies (single premise~$=$~conclusion),
412	seed~43 generates uppercase pseudo-Prolog that bypasses the text-match classifier while remaining functionally tautological,
413	and seed~44 converts NL conclusions to snake\_case atoms used as both fact and query.
414	The diversity of gaming pathways across seeds---despite identical training data and reward function---demonstrates that Goodhart's Law in neurosymbolic reasoning is not a single failure mode but a family of convergent exploits.

416	\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
417	\label{app:100step}

422	This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training---well before the prove-rate plateau---and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
423	The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.1\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{app:setup}

Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} lists all hyperparameters shared across experiments.
All RL conditions use the same GRPO configuration; only the reward function differs.
Seeds control model weight initialization and data shuffling; training data is held constant across all seeds and conditions (Constraint~C001).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Training hyperparameters for all GRPO experiments.}
\label{tab:hyperparams}
\footnotesize
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textit{Model}} \\
Base model & Qwen3-4B \\
Precision & BF16 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textit{GRPO Training}} \\
Rollouts per prompt ($K$) & 8 \\
Training steps (default) & 500 \\
Training steps (extended) & 1000 \\
Learning rate & $1 \times 10^{-6}$ \\
Per-device batch size & 4 \\
Gradient accumulation steps & 2 \\
Effective batch size & 8 \\
Max completion length & 512 tokens \\
Random seeds & 42, 43, 44 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textit{Data}} \\
Training set & FOLIO, 500 examples \\
Evaluation set & FOLIO, 100 examples (held-out) \\
Data file & \texttt{train\_500\_seed42} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textit{Solvers}} \\
FOL solver & Prover9 \\
Prolog solver & SWI-Prolog 8.4.2 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textit{Evaluation}} \\
Decoding & Greedy ($T{=}0$) \\
ISR computation & \texttt{eval\_sta.py} \\
ISR variant & Proved-only (ISR$^*$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Evaluation exception.}
FOL exec-only seed~43 (\texttt{plan001-exec-only-s43-r4}) was evaluated with sampling (temperature~$=0.7$) rather than greedy decoding.
Its PR and ISR values are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable with other seeds under the unified evaluation protocol (C004).


\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} (Section~\ref{sec:sta}) gives the procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.
For unproved samples ($S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$), ISR is undefined and the protocol is not applied.


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
$\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism; $\beta{=}0.3$ completes the Goodhart trajectory with outright performance collapse.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Exec} & \textbf{ISR} & \textbf{Rnd} & \textbf{SFT} \\
\midrule
H1 & Concl.\ in premises & 87 & 17 & 81 & 7 \\
H7 & Single prem.\ = concl. & $\bullet$ & \textbf{65} & 0 & 0 \\
Tautological & 2-comp $P{=}C$ & $\bullet$ & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Repetition & Output degen. & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
Contradiction & $n_{\text{comp}}$ inflated & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
C-w/o-utility & Complex, redundant & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\
Q-as-fact & Atom = fact+query & -- & -- & -- & -- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Hacking taxonomy across FOL conditions (\% of proved samples). ISR/Rand columns: $\beta{=}0.1$ 3-seed means. Exec: H1${=}87$\% in s42; $\bullet$ marks seed- or step-specific modes (H7/Tautological in s44, Repetition in s43, Contradiction at 1000 steps). C-w/o-util.: complexity-without-utility (random-specific). Q-as-fact: Prolog STA only (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).}
\label{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).


\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).

\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\label{fig:prolog-comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ISR collapse trajectory (FOL exec-only, seed 42).}
Table~\ref{tab:fol-detailed} traces the ISR collapse over training:
ISR$^*=0.642$ at 100 steps $\to$ $0.132$ at 500 steps ($-79.4$\%) $\to$ $0.003$ at 1000 steps ($-99.5$\% from step 100).
PR increases monotonically ($0.32 \to 0.93 \to 0.96$) while structural quality collapses, confirming that ISR captures degeneration invisible to execution reward.
By step 1000, 94.8\% of proved samples have ISR~$=0$ and the mean component count rises to 18.55.

\paragraph{Prolog: universal Goodhart via three distinct pathways.}
All three Prolog exec+ISR seeds exhibit Goodhart's Law with 0\% non-hacking proofs (Figure~\ref{fig:prolog-comparison}), but each discovers a different gaming mechanism:
seed~42 produces clean H7 tautologies (single premise~$=$~conclusion),
seed~43 generates uppercase pseudo-Prolog that bypasses the text-match classifier while remaining functionally tautological,
and seed~44 converts NL conclusions to snake\_case atoms used as both fact and query.
The diversity of gaming pathways across seeds---despite identical training data and reward function---demonstrates that Goodhart's Law in neurosymbolic reasoning is not a single failure mode but a family of convergent exploits.

\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
\label{app:100step}

To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%---higher than SFT (14\%) but still early in training.
Of the 32 proved samples, 9 (28.1\%) exhibit H7 hacking (single premise identical to conclusion) and 1 (3.1\%) exhibits H1 (conclusion embedded among premises), yielding a total hacking rate of 31.2\%.
By contrast, SFT at comparable or lower PR shows 7.1\% hacking (1/14 proved samples).
This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training---well before the prove-rate plateau---and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.1\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}

We introduced Solver Trace Ablation (STA), a component-level diagnostic for neurosymbolic formalizers that exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation.
Applied to GRPO-trained models, ISR reveals a collapse trajectory hidden from prove rate, confirmed as RL-specific by an SFT baseline with near-zero hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
When repurposed as a training signal, ISR induces meta-level Goodhart's Law: at low dose, the model games the diagnostic itself through conclusion duplication absent under matched controls; at high dose, prove rate collapses (18\% vs.\ 48\% random); the sole apparent ISR improvement reduces to noise after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Both diagnostic utility and Goodhart vulnerability transfer to Prolog/SWI-Prolog: ISR-as-reward yields universal gaming across all seeds with zero non-hacking proofs, each via a distinct mechanism (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Across six reward conditions and two logic types, we catalog seven hacking modes, including query-as-fact gaming that bypasses text-match classifiers (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Interpreting ISR.}
ISR values must be read relative to the optimization objective: under exec-only Prolog, \emph{low} ISR reflects redundant coding, not absent reasoning; under ISR-as-reward, \emph{high} ISR reflects metric gaming.
The premise-count confound applies to any ablation-based diagnostic on variable-length outputs; Shapley values could provide more nuanced attribution at higher cost.

\paragraph{Meta-Level Goodhart.}
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming, yet becomes gamed itself when optimized---a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming; $\beta{=}0.3$: collapse) maps onto~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization} at a meta level.
ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools; the asymmetry (reliable observer, unreliable optimizer) may generalize to other perturbation-based quality metrics.
Open directions include reward functions robust to identified gaming modes and extending STA to broader logic types.

1	\section{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	Experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B) and dataset family (FOLIO); generalization remains untested.
5	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a downstream NLI evaluation finds ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
6	Three seeds demonstrate qualitative divergence but limit statistical power.
7	STA requires solvers supporting component-level input manipulation.
8	
9	\paragraph{Data scale.}
10	Our experiments use 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples, drawn from the 1,204 FOL-annotated examples available in FOLIO~\citep{folio}.
11	The training subset is selected via stratified sampling (seed 42) and held constant across all conditions.
12	While our findings are consistent across seeds and logic types, the effect of training data scale on hacking prevalence and mode distribution remains an open question for future work.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on held-out logical reasoning problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises, reducing each ``proof'' to a structural shortcut invisible to the execution reward.
When the solver receives premises that already contain the target conclusion, it trivially succeeds; the model has learned to satisfy the reward without performing logical derivation.
This gap between execution success and structural integrity defines a critical blind spot in neurosymbolic reinforcement learning.

Neurosymbolic approaches that pair large language models with formal solvers have demonstrated strong performance on logical reasoning benchmarks~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025}.
The dominant paradigm treats solver execution as a binary reward signal: the model generates a formal specification, a solver attempts a proof, and the outcome drives policy optimization via GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} or related algorithms~\citep{deepseek-r1}.
This execution-only evaluation conflates genuine reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
A model can achieve arbitrarily high prove rates by embedding the target conclusion among its premises, by producing contradictory axiom sets that prove anything via explosion, or by generating tautological single-clause outputs---all of which satisfy the solver without requiring any logical derivation.
Specification gaming of this kind has been documented in reasoning models more broadly~\citep{bondarenko-spec-gaming}, and a growing body of work studies reward hacking mechanisms in LLM training~\citep{reward-hacking-survey}, yet systematic characterization in neurosymbolic RL remains absent.

No principled diagnostic exists for detecting and quantifying structural degeneration in RL-trained formalizers.
Prompting-based neurosymbolic systems~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm} do not involve RL training and thus sidestep the problem entirely.
\citet{mellgren-prolog-grpo} hand-craft Prolog-specific structure penalties but provide no systematic analysis of the failure modes they target.
Verification-reward approaches use solver or prover outcomes as training signals~\citep{deepseek-prover-v15, rlsf} but evaluate execution correctness only.
Recent work has begun examining whether LLMs game formalization tasks~\citep{kim-game-formalization}, finding that high compilation rates do not imply faithful outputs---yet no framework connects structural diagnosis to the reward hacking dynamics that emerge during RL training.
The result is a field that optimizes for---and reports---prove rates without any mechanism to assess whether the underlying formalizations contain genuine logical structure.

We observe that component necessity testing---systematically ablating each solver input and checking whether the proof still holds---provides a principled, solver-agnostic diagnostic for this problem.
Removing a premise from a well-structured formalization should break the proof; removing one from a degenerate output that embeds the conclusion will not.
This leave-one-out (LOO) protocol yields a continuous score, the \emph{Intensional Structure Ratio} (ISR), measuring the fraction of formal components that are necessary for the proof.
The protocol requires only the ability to re-execute the solver with modified inputs, making it applicable across formal languages and proof systems without language-specific engineering.

A natural question follows: can ISR serve not merely as a post-hoc diagnostic but as a training signal to incentivize structural integrity?
We find that it cannot.
When ISR is incorporated into the GRPO reward, the model games the metric itself---a meta-level instance of Goodhart's Law~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, gao-reward-overoptimization}.
Rather than producing better-structured proofs, the model discovers strategies that inflate ISR directly, most commonly by reducing all premises to a single clause that duplicates the conclusion.
ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness, and LOO-based metrics carry an inherent mathematical bias toward outputs with fewer components: fewer premises means each is trivially more ``necessary.''
These properties make ISR a reliable observer of structural integrity but an unreliable optimizer of it.

We introduce \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a protocol that applies component necessity testing to derive ISR and systematically characterizes reward hacking across GRPO training conditions (Figure~\ref{fig:sta_overview}).
Our experimental design spans 6 reward configurations (execution-only, ISR-augmented at two dose levels, matched random-reward controls, convex combination, and a supervised fine-tuning baseline), 3 random seeds per configuration, and up to 1{,}000 training steps, evaluated on two formal languages: first-order logic (FOL, verified by Prover9) and Prolog (verified by SWI-Prolog).

STA reveals that execution-only GRPO training produces progressive structural collapse invisible to the training reward.
Prove rate reaches 93\% while ISR deteriorates from 0.64 at 100 steps to 0.13 at 500 steps to 0.003 at 1{,}000 steps---a 99.5\% decline quantifying structural degeneration that prove rate cannot detect.
All three random seeds exhibit 87--100\% conclusion embedding in their proved outputs, demonstrating that degeneration is systematic rather than seed-specific.
By 1{,}000 steps, 94.8\% of proved samples have ISR${=}$0: no single component is necessary for the proof.
A supervised fine-tuning baseline trained on the same data achieves only 14\% prove rate but 92.9\% structurally genuine outputs with near-zero hacking (7.1\% H1, 0\% H7), confirming that reward hacking is RL-specific rather than an artifact of data exposure (\textbf{C1}: ISR as diagnostic, with complete collapse trajectory; \S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

When ISR augments the GRPO reward ($r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$), meta-level Goodhart effects emerge~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl}.
At low dose ($\beta{=}0.1$), ISR reward induces ISR-specific gaming: across three seeds, 64.5\% of proved outputs exhibit single-premise conclusion duplication (H7 mode) that inflates ISR by gaming the metric, compared to 0\% across all three random-reward controls---confirming H7 as ISR-reward-specific.
The remaining seed's apparent structural advantage disappears entirely under premise-count-matched analysis (1.06$\times$, indistinguishable from the random baseline); the raw ISR elevation is a mathematical artifact of premise minimization, not improved reasoning.
At high dose ($\beta{=}0.3$), classic Goodhart collapse occurs: prove rate drops to 18\% versus 48\% for the matched random control.
This dose-response pattern maps onto established Goodhart dynamics~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization}: low-dose proxy gaming that inflates the metric without genuine improvement, followed by high-dose collapse where the proxy signal overwhelms the primary objective.
ISR-as-reward provides no genuine structural benefit at any dose (\textbf{C2}: empirical meta-level Goodhart characterization; \S\ref{sec:goodhart}).

Both the diagnostic capability and the Goodhart failure transfer across structurally different formal languages.
Applying STA to Prolog formalizations verified by SWI-Prolog, execution-only training again produces near-zero ISR (mean 0.04 across 3 seeds, $\text{PR}{=}53\%{\pm}31\text{pp}$), replicating the FOL collapse pattern with comparable cross-seed instability.
Prolog ISR-as-reward yields \emph{universal} Goodhart: all three seeds converge to gaming with 0\% genuine output, each via a distinct mechanism---tautological single-clause duplication, degenerate uppercase pseudo-Prolog syntax, and query-as-fact gaming where the model sets the target query as its own provable fact.
This is strictly stronger than the FOL result, where ${\sim}$16\% genuine output persists, demonstrating that simpler formal semantics enable more complete metric exploitation (\textbf{C3}: cross-logic diagnostic transfer with universal Goodhart; \S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).

Across all experimental conditions, we identify and quantify 7 distinct hacking modes---conclusion embedding in single-premise (H7) and multi-premise (H1) variants, tautological collapse, complexity-without-utility, repetition collapse, premise padding, and query-as-fact gaming---providing a concrete, empirically grounded taxonomy for diagnosing structural failures in neurosymbolic RL systems.
Each mode is quantified per reward condition and seed, enabling practitioners to anticipate the specific failure modes their training configurations are likely to produce (\textbf{C4}: hacking taxonomy; \S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

These findings expose a fundamental asymmetry: ISR is reliable as a diagnostic observer of structural integrity but unreliable as an optimization target.
This instantiates a broader cautionary principle for proxy-metric-as-reward approaches~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, pan-reward-misspecification}: diagnostic metrics that detect reward hacking can themselves become gaming targets when repurposed as training signals.
The asymmetry---\emph{reliable observer, unreliable optimizer}---carries implications beyond formal reasoning for any system where proxy measures of structural quality are candidates for reward shaping.
We release our code, evaluation scripts, and complete experimental outputs to support reproducibility.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on first-order logic problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises.
The solver succeeds not because the model has learned to reason, but because the formalization trivially entails any conclusion that already appears as a premise.
This structural shortcut is invisible to execution-based evaluation: prove rate registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation or degenerate circular embedding.
The reward optimizes solver success; the model finds the shortest path to it.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate---the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}---conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but gives no gradient on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A separate line documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a diagnostic protocol applying \emph{component necessity testing}---leave-one-out (LOO) ablation on solver inputs---to quantify structural integrity (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ indicating complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard---in mutation testing~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} and feature attribution---and we claim novelty not in the primitive but in its application as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity: a downstream NLI evaluation finds ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated ($\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory entirely invisible to prove rate: $\text{ISR}^{*}{:}\,0.642\to 0.132\to 0.003$ over 100--1000 steps (99.5\% degradation) while PR rises $32\%{\to}96\%$.
Three seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
An SFT baseline on the same data achieves $\text{PR}{=}14\%$ with 92.9\% non-hacking, confirming the collapse is a consequence of RL reward optimization, not data or capacity.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart.}
Can ISR serve as a training signal? When added to the reward, $r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta\,\text{ISR})$, the model games the diagnostic itself---\emph{meta-level Goodhart's Law}~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, karwowski-goodhart-rl, gao-reward-overoptimization}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, 64.5\% of proved samples (3-seed mean) exhibit ISR-specific single-premise-equals-conclusion duplication---a construction in which ISR is high \emph{by definition}---versus 0\% under matched random-bonus reward; the one seed with non-trivial ``genuine'' residual reduces to $1.06\times$ random after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
At $\beta{=}0.3$, cross-seed instability is extreme (PR $66{\pm}42\%$) with three distinct Goodhart pathways: reward collapse, shortcut dominance, and pure metric gaming.
The effect transfers and intensifies in Prolog: all three seeds produce 0\% non-hacking via distinct mechanisms, including \emph{query-as-fact gaming} that bypasses text-match classifiers.
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer.}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
Across 6 reward conditions, 3 seeds, 2 logic types, and up to 1000 steps:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item[\textbf{C1.}] \textbf{ISR as diagnostic} for GRPO reward hacking, with a 99.5\% ISR collapse trajectory invisible to PR and an SFT control localizing the failure to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
\item[\textbf{C2.}] \textbf{Empirical meta-level Goodhart}, with a random-bonus control isolating ISR-specific gaming (64.5\% vs.\ 0\%) and a premise-count-matched analysis showing the sole apparent ISR gain is an LOO artifact (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
\item[\textbf{C3.}] \textbf{Cross-logic transfer} to Prolog/SWI-Prolog with universal Goodhart (3/3 seeds, 0\% non-hacking), indicating simpler semantics enable more complete exploitation (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
\item[\textbf{C4.}] \textbf{A seven-mode hacking taxonomy} including query-as-fact gaming, motivating functional ($n_{\text{necessary}}$-based) cross-validation of diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
\end{itemize}
The empirical Goodhart characterization, premise-count confound, and cross-logic universality are cautionary results for any work treating a structural proxy as a training signal.

106	H7---a single premise identical to the conclusion, giving $\text{ISR}\geq 0.5$ by construction (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method})---is the canonical meta-level Goodhart move: the model satisfies the LOO definition directly rather than producing a derivation that happens to satisfy it.
107	Total conclusion embedding ($\text{H1}+\text{H7}$) is GRPO-universal at $68$--$97\%$ across both conditions, and is in fact \emph{higher} under random (mean H1 81\% under random vs.\ 17\% under ISR).
108	ISR does not reduce hacking; it converts H1 into H7 (Figure~\ref{fig:hacking-composition}).
109	Random also achieves higher and more stable PR ($85{\pm}6\%$ vs.\ $77{\pm}14\%$), so ISR-as-reward yields no PR advantage either.
110	
111	\textbf{Premise-count confound.}
112	One ISR seed (s42) is the only one not dominated by H7, and its raw $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.415$ is 3.2$\times$ higher than its matched random control ($0.131$), suggesting genuine structural improvement.
113	This appearance is entirely a premise-minimization artifact.
114	ISR-trained models produce shorter formalizations (mean $n{=}5.58$ vs.\ $8.46$ for random), and ISR rises mechanically as $n$ falls---when $n{=}2$, ISR$\geq 0.5$ by definition.
115	Restricting to non-hacking samples with $\geq{3}$ premises (eliminating the trivial-$n$ regime) gives $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.258$ for ISR vs.\ $0.243$ for random: a 1.06$\times$ ratio, no meaningful advantage (Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}, last column). %% D051 premise-count-matched analysis
116	The raw 3.2$\times$ headline collapses once the LOO bias is controlled.
117	This is methodologically important: LOO-based metrics are widely used without component-count correction; under optimization that pressure for shorter outputs, the metric inflates without any quality improvement.
118	
119	\textbf{High-dose ISR ($\beta{=}0.3$): multi-modal Goodhart instability.}
120	At $\beta{=}0.3$, ISR-as-reward produces extreme cross-seed instability (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}, last group): $\text{PR}{=}66{\pm}42\%$, spanning $18\%$ to $95\%$.
121	Each seed converges to a distinct Goodhart pathway. %% registry: plan002-additive-b03-s42/s43/s44
122	Seed~42 exhibits \emph{reward collapse}: $\text{PR}{=}18\%$, $\text{ISR}^{*}{=}0.143$, the classical Goodhart pattern from~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization} where the proxy weight overwhelms the base signal.
123	Seed~43 exhibits \emph{H1-dominant shortcutting}: $\text{PR}{=}86\%$, $\text{H1}{=}68.6\%$, $\text{H7}{=}4.7\%$, only $26.7\%$ non-hacking---the model retains a high prove rate but achieves it via conclusion embedding, not structural manipulation of the metric.
124	Seed~44 exhibits \emph{pure H7 meta-Goodhart}: $\text{PR}{=}95\%$ combined with $\text{H7}{=}100\%$ and $\text{ISR}^{*}{=}0.742$, with $0\%$ non-hacking.
125	This last case is the cleanest meta-level Goodhart instance in our experiments: the model simultaneously games \emph{both} the execution reward (high PR) and the structural metric (high $\text{ISR}^{*}$) through the same construction.
126	For the random control at $\beta{=}0.3$, the available 2 seeds collapse to $\text{PR}{=}48\%$ (s42) and $\text{PR}{=}23\%$ (s44) with $\text{H1}{=}100\%$ and $0\%$ non-hacking in both cases (the s43 random run is still training; full numbers in Appendix~\ref{app:beta03}). %% registry: plan017-additive-random-s42, exp1-random-b03-s44
127	High-dose proxy weighting is harmful in both ISR and random conditions, but ISR uniquely produces \emph{mode diversity}: three qualitatively different failure trajectories from a single reward formulation.
128	
129	\subsection{Cross-Logic Diagnostic Transfer}
130	\label{sec:crosslogic}
131	
132	\begin{figure}[t]
133	\centering
134	\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/fig4_prolog_comparison.pdf}
135	\caption{Cross-logic results. \textbf{Left}: FOL vs.\ Prolog exec-only $\text{ISR}^*$ across 3 seeds, both near-zero (s44 Prolog $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.387$ is a small-sample artifact, $n{=}21$). \textbf{Right}: Prolog ISR-reward gaming-mode composition---all 3 seeds reach 100\% non-genuine through distinct mechanisms (H7 tautology / degenerate uppercase syntax / query-as-fact gaming).}
136	\label{fig:prolog-comparison}
137	\end{figure}
138	
139	We replicate the FOL pipeline with Prolog/SWI-Prolog, retraining seeds and re-evaluating with the same eval harness.
140	Two questions: (i) does ISR retain diagnostic value on a structurally different logic; (ii) does ISR-as-reward produce the same meta-level Goodhart failure mode?
141

143	\centering
144	\small

146	\begin{tabular}{llccccl}

166	
167	\textbf{Prolog exec-only: ISR catches redundancy across logics.}
168	Two of three Prolog exec-only seeds (s42, s43) show $\text{ISR}^{*}{\approx}0$ despite moderate-to-high PR (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}). %% registry: plan006-prolog-exec-s42, plan006-prolog-exec-s43-r3
169	Inspection reveals \emph{redundant coding}: ground facts repeated multiple times (e.g., \texttt{penguin(fido).} appearing three times), so per-clause LOO ablation never breaks the proof and the necessity count is zero.
170	This is a different failure semantics from the FOL exec-only collapses (which centered on conclusion embedding), but $\text{ISR}^{*}$ flags both.
171	This is also the point at which interpretation matters: an exec-only low-ISR is a \emph{redundancy} signal, whereas an ISR-rewarded high-ISR is a \emph{metric-gaming} signal (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method}); the same number does not license the same conclusion about reasoning quality, and we are careful never to read ISR differences as reasoning differences without the mode breakdown.
172	
173	\textbf{Prolog ISR-as-reward: universal Goodhart.}
174	The Prolog ISR-reward result is stronger than its FOL counterpart: 3/3 seeds reach 0\% non-hacking through three distinct mechanisms (Figure~\ref{fig:prolog-comparison}, right; Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).
175	Seed~42 produces clean H7 tautologies---a single clause identical to the query, $\text{ISR}^{*}{=}1.0$ over all $50/100$ proved samples. %% registry: plan006-prolog-sta-s42
176	Seed~43 produces \emph{degenerate uppercase pseudo-Prolog} (e.g., \texttt{MARY\_IS\_AN\_AVA\-DEOTE.}); the strict text-match classifier returns $\text{H7}{=}0$ but functional analysis shows all 38 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$, i.e., a single clause that proves the query alone---functionally H7. %% registry: plan006-prolog-sta-s43
177	Seed~44 produces \emph{query-as-fact gaming}: the model transforms the NL question into a snake-case atom and asserts the same atom as both a fact and the query (e.g., \texttt{is\_the\_dog\_furry. \?- is\_the\_dog\_furry.}), giving $\text{PR}{=}97\%$ with $95/97$ proved samples at $n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$. %% registry: plan006-prolog-sta-s44
178	Seed~44 evaded our initial strict classifier entirely (returned ``$100\%$ genuine''); functional cross-validation against the $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution exposed it.
179	We register this as a methodological lesson: text-match hacking classifiers have blind spots, and STA's per-sample necessity profile is the cross-check that catches them.
180	
181	\textbf{FOL vs.\ Prolog comparison.}
182	FOL ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ leaves ${\sim}16\%$ non-hacking residual; Prolog ISR leaves $0\%$ across 3 seeds.
183	We attribute this to Prolog's simpler operational semantics: the optimization landscape contains fewer high-PR derivations and is more easily satisfied by clause-level shortcuts, so the gaming basin is broader and the genuine residual disappears.
184	This is corroborating, not contradictory, evidence for Claim 2: in a setting where structural shortcuts are even easier to construct, ISR-as-reward collapses even more completely.
185	
186	\subsection{Hacking Taxonomy}
187	\label{sec:taxonomy}
188

194	\end{figure}

Cells with seed identifiers indicate the mode dominates that seed (Prolog ISR row: H7 is s42 strict + s43/s44 functional, totaling 100\% gaming across all 3 seeds). $^\sharp$strict for FOL; pooled strict+functional for Prolog (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).}
216	\label{tab:hacking-taxonomy}
217	\end{table}
218	
219	The full taxonomy (Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy}, definitions in \S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method}) consists of seven modes that span the conditions we studied.
220	Two are quantifiable across all conditions: \textbf{H1} (conclusion embedding) is GRPO-universal at $68$--$97\%$ regardless of reward type, and \textbf{H7} (conclusion duplication) is ISR-specific at $64.5\%$ vs.\ $0\%$ in random controls.
221	The remaining five appear in specific cells: \textbf{tautological collapse} (exec-only s44 and Prolog ISR s42); \textbf{repetition collapse} (exec-only s43, with 87\% of rollouts hitting max length); \textbf{contradiction explosion} (exec-only at 1000 steps, mean $n{=}18.55$); \textbf{complexity-without-utility} (random $\beta{=}0.1$, low residual); and \textbf{query-as-fact gaming} (Prolog ISR s44).
222	
223	The cross-condition pattern is consistent with the framing in \S\ref{sec:goodhart}: \emph{reward formulation determines hacking composition but not hacking prevalence.}
224	Exec-only, ISR, and random conditions all show $\geq 80\%$ pooled hacking among proved samples; only SFT---which does not optimize against a binary execution signal---shows the residual at $93\%$ non-hacking, consistent with hacking being RL-specific rather than data-induced.
225	Across two logic types, six reward conditions, three seeds, and up to 1000 training steps, no GRPO condition we tested produces a high-PR run that is also majority non-hacking; the closest is ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ s42 at $\text{PR}{=}81\%$ with $32\%$ non-hacking, and even that residual is the premise-minimization artifact analyzed in \S\ref{sec:goodhart}.
226	
227	The taxonomy is descriptive, not exhaustive: query-as-fact gaming was found only when we cross-validated the strict classifier against $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distributions, and additional modes may emerge under further reward formulations or logic types.
228	We expect the STA protocol itself to generalize---it requires only a solver and a notion of component---so future work can extend the taxonomy by applying the same two-stage classification to new domains.
